The blue gets lost along the way, and it's the red and orange that remain.

sentences: Ten years ago, many announced the death of radio.
Young people no longer listened to it; television and the internet had won.
And yet, radio did not die out: it reinvented itself in another form.
Today, millions of people listen to podcasts every day, these audio shows that you download and listen to whenever you want.
The first advantage of podcasts is their freedom.
Unlike traditional radio, there are no more schedules.
The show waits for you, not the other way around.
You can pause, rewind, or speed up.
This flexibility perfectly matches our fragmented lives, where free time comes in small bits.
The second advantage is that it frees up your eyes and hands.
You listen to a podcast while cooking, ironing, driving, or running.
Moments that were once empty or boring become moments of learning or escape.
My daily tram ride, for example, has become my appointment with a history show.
Twenty minutes of waiting turned into twenty minutes of pleasure.
We also need to talk about variety.
There are podcasts on absolutely everything: philosophy, crime, parenting, gardening, economics, and listeners' love stories.
Professional shows sit alongside amateur creations recorded in a bedroom.
This diversity would be impossible on traditional radio, limited by its programming schedules.
But the real secret of podcasts might be elsewhere: in the intimacy of the voice.
Listening to someone through headphones is like having them close to you.
No images, no sets, just a voice that speaks to you.
Many listeners develop a strange bond with their favorite hosts: you feel like you know these people, like you're meeting friends each week.
Some worry: by constantly having our ears occupied, are we losing silence, daydreaming, and fertile boredom?
The question is worth asking.
As always, it's all a matter of balance.
If you've never tried it, the instructions are simple: choose a topic you’re passionate about, search, and listen.
The first episode is rarely the right one; the third one often hooks you.
Radio is not dead.
It has slipped into our pockets, and it has never been better.

sentences: Try this test: the next time you wait for the bus, look around you.
How many people are just looking at the street?
None, or almost none.
All eyes are down on a screen.
Even the slightest empty minute is quickly filled.
Without realizing it, we have made something disappear from our lives: boredom.
Good riddance, you might say.
Boredom has never had a good reputation.
Doing nothing, in our culture, is wasting time.
You have to be productive, active, efficient — and when you're not working, you should at least 'enjoy' yourself, which is still a form of activity.
Someone who stares at the ceiling is seen as lazy.
And yet.
Researchers studying the brain have made an interesting discovery: when we do 'nothing', our brain doesn't stop at all.
It enters a particular mode that scientists call the 'default network'.
It's precisely in this mode that it sorts memories, makes connections between ideas, and imagines the future.
In other words: it's when we do nothing that our ideas are formed.
Experience confirms this even without a laboratory.
Where do your best ideas come to you?
Rarely in front of the computer, while fully concentrating.
Almost always in the shower, while walking, or looking out the window of a train.
These moments have one thing in common: the mind is free there, with no task to accomplish.
Archimedes, it is said, had his idea in the bath — not at his desk.
Children also teach us a lesson.
Let a child be bored, resist the urge to suggest an activity, and observe.
After a phase of complaints — 'I'm so bored' — they always end up inventing something: a game, a story, a fort.
Boredom is the starting point of imagination.
By filling every minute of our children’s time, and our own, we eliminate this starting point.
So, what to do — or rather, what not to do?
I started a small exercise, almost ridiculously simple: every day, ten minutes sitting, without a phone, without a book, without music.
Just looking out the window.
The first few days were surprisingly uncomfortable; my hand reached for the phone on its own.
Then calm came, and with it, thoughts I never had time to have.
I'm not saying you should be bored all day.
I'm saying that a little emptiness, in a life that is too full, is not wasted time.
It might be the best time spent in the day.

sentences: Why learn dates, poems, and multiplication tables when all of that can be found in three seconds in our pocket? This argument is heard everywhere, and it's not foolish.
It even reflects a valid intuition of our time: at a moment when an infinite library fits in a phone, human memory seems to have lost its job.
However, upon closer examination, this quick conclusion seems to rest on a deep misunderstanding of what it means to think.
First, let's acknowledge what is true about the argument.
It would be absurd to make a student memorize a directory or a list that a machine can instantly retrieve.

For a long time, schools have confused instruction with recitation, and they were partly right to move away from that to develop analysis, critical thinking, and the ability to search for and sort information.
A brain turned into a simple hard drive is a waste; on this point, opponents of 'learning by heart' have made a valid point.
But they make a crucial confusion: they believe that one can think without knowing anything, think in a vacuum, reason about content that one would go and look for as needed.
But that is false, and cognitive sciences clearly confirm it.
To understand new information, one must attach it to knowledge already present in the mind.
Read an article on a subject you know nothing about: the words flow by, but nothing sticks, due to a lack of hooks to hang the meaning on.
In contrast, the expert reads the same text and grasps every nuance because their internal knowledge provides the context.
Stored knowledge is not the enemy of reflection: it is its condition.
We do not think despite what we know; we think with it.
There’s more.
Constantly consulting a screen has a hidden cost.

Every interruption to check a piece of information breaks the thread of reasoning; the mind that has to search for everything never has enough materials available to establish quick links, those sudden connections from which ideas emerge.
The scholar who has a thousand facts from their field 'in mind' sees connections invisible to someone who has to look for them one by one.
Creativity feeds on what is immediately there, in the mind, ready to combine.
Finally, there’s what the utilitarian argument completely overlooks: some knowledge serves no purpose, and that is precisely its value.
A poem learned in childhood accompanies us throughout life, returning on a night of sadness or happiness, connecting us to those who knew it before us.
Knowledge is not just a tool; it is also companionship, shared culture, a part of ourselves that no screen will ever replace.
The right question is therefore not 'memory or reflection?' — a false opposition — but 'what is worth knowing by heart?'.
To this question, each era must respond anew.
Ours would be wrong to answer 'nothing'.

sentences: Few questions cause as much anxiety and guilt among parents as the issue of screens.
Should they be banned?
Should they be limited?
From what age, and for how long?
Between alarmist articles that describe a generation in peril and those who shrug it off by reminding us that 'every generation demonizes its novelty,' parents struggle to find their way.
Let's try to clarify things by separating what research establishes from what it does not say.
On one point, the data is solid: for very young children, before the age of two or three, excessive screen time is harmful.
At this age, the brain develops through interaction with the real world and with people: manipulating objects, hearing speech, exchanging glances and smiles.
Time spent in front of a screen is time taken away from these irreplaceable experiences, and several studies link early excessive exposure to delays in language and concentration.
For toddlers, the caution in recommendations — as little as possible — is based on solid grounds.
But as soon as we move past early childhood, the question becomes murky, and this is where public debate often goes wrong.
Because 'screens' do not exist: there are only radically different uses.

Putting in the same category a child who passively watches endless videos, another who calls their grandparents, a third who learns to code or draws on a tablet, and a fourth who plays online with friends makes no sense.
The 'screen time' counter, so convenient, is a crude measure that adds together incomparable things.
The real question is not just how much time, but what, at what age, and with whom.
This last point — with whom — is crucial and too often overlooked.
The same program watched alone in silence, or watched with an adult who comments, explains, and extends the conversation, does not have the same effect at all.
In the latter case, the screen becomes a medium for exchange rather than a substitute for relationships.
It's not the object that matters most; it's what happens around it.
We must also place the screen within the context of a child's entire life.
The problem is not so much what the screen provides but what it replaces when it takes up too much space: shortened sleep, free play, fertile boredom, physical activity, and friendships in person.
A child who reads, runs, plays, sleeps well, and sees friends can watch a screen without harm; danger arises when the screen pushes everything else out.
Finally, example weighs more than rules.
It's hard to convince a teenager to look up from their phone when their parents have their noses in theirs at the table.
Children imitate what we do, not what we say.
The reasonable response is therefore neither panic nor indifference, but attention.
Not just 'how many hours?' as the only compass, but 'what content, at what age, replacing what, and under whose gaze?'.
It's more demanding than a simple rule.
It's also much fairer.

sentences: When we think about protecting the environment, we often imagine sorting waste or renewable energy.
We forget a more discreet but essential cause: the way we consume.
Because every item we buy requires energy, water, and raw materials to be made, long before it reaches our hands.
Reducing our consumption is therefore one of the most effective actions — and one of the most difficult.
The problem has a name: overconsumption.
We are buying more than ever, often items designed not to last.

A piece of clothing worn three times and then forgotten, a device that breaks down just after the warranty and can't be repaired, a phone replaced even though the old one was still working: this disposable model has become the norm.
It enriches the industry, but it depletes the planet and fills our landfills.
Consuming differently doesn't mean buying nothing, which would be unrealistic.
It means buying better and less.
A few simple principles are enough to change things.
First, ask yourself if you really need the item before buying it.
Then, prioritize quality: a solid and repairable item costs more upfront, but lasts for years, and is therefore cheaper in the long run — for us as well as for the environment.
Finally, rediscover second-hand: buying used is giving a second life to an item that already exists, without making a new one.
However, this change faces a powerful force: marketing, which tirelessly works to make us desire new things.
Fashion itself is based on this logic: what was perfect last year suddenly becomes 'outdated.'
Resisting this pressure requires a certain freedom of mind — the freedom not to let advertising dictate our needs.
Consuming more responsibly is not a sacrifice, and it is also not the only solution to the ecological problem.
But it is a choice that makes sense, and it has an unexpected advantage: it also lightens our lives.
Fewer items mean less clutter, less spending, and fewer things to organize and maintain.
By taking care of the planet, we often end up taking care of ourselves.

sentences: It's December, and like every year, I'm thinking about next year.
This time, I want to do things differently.
Usually, I make a long list in January: exercise, eat better, read more, learn Spanish, tidy up the house, save money.
The result: by March, I haven't done anything at all.
Too many projects at the same time is like having no project at all.
So this year, I've chosen only three things.
First, I'm going to sign up for an accounting course.
My job is going to change, and I will need this knowledge.
The classes start in February, on Tuesday evenings, for four months.
Next, I'm going to go on a trip with my sister.
We've been talking about it for six years, without ever doing it.
This time, we've already chosen the dates: the first week of September.
We're going to book in January, so that it's decided.
Finally, and this is the smallest project, I'm going to the dentist.
I've been putting off this appointment for two years.
Three projects is few.
But each one has a date, and that's new for me.
My sister asked me why 'exercise' wasn't on the list.
I replied: 'Because I've been putting it on for ten years.'

sentences: When Tom arrived in France to work, several things surprised him.
The first one is the holidays.
In France, all employees have at least five weeks of paid leave per year.
Many companies even give a little more.
In the United Kingdom, the legal minimum is about four weeks, including public holidays.
The second surprise is the legal working time: thirty-five hours per week.
That doesn't mean that no one works more.
But beyond that, those are overtime hours, which must be paid or compensated.
The third surprise concerns evening emails.
In his previous job in London, Tom received messages at ten o'clock in the evening and he would reply to them.
It was normal.
In France, there has been a 'right to disconnect' since 2017.
Companies must respect their employees' rest time outside of working hours.
The first time Tom sent a message on a Sunday, a colleague replied to him on Monday morning: 'On Sundays, I don't read my messages.'
Tom took it badly at first.
Then he understood that it wasn't a criticism.
Today, he turns off his computer at six o'clock.
'It's the best habit that France has given me,' he says.

sentences: France protects several tens of thousands of historic monuments, from cathedrals to village washhouses.
This policy is old: it dates back to the nineteenth century, at a time when many medieval buildings were being destroyed or looted.
It raises a question that is rarely asked: who decides what is worth preserving?
The classification follows precise procedures, with experts and commissions.
But every choice of conservation is also a choice of narrative.
For a long time, priority was given to protecting castles, churches, and aristocratic homes — that is, the traces of the powerful.
The buildings of ordinary work, on the other hand, have largely disappeared: workshops, factories, farms, workers' housing.
In recent decades, this perspective has changed.
Industrial heritage is now recognized, and old factories are being transformed into museums, housing, or cultural venues rather than being demolished.
The question of cost remains.
The maintenance of a monument is ongoing, and many rural communities have churches that they cannot afford to restore.
The number of endangered buildings is significant.
The solutions are varied: dedicated lotteries, sponsorship, crowdfunding, repurposing for another use.
This last avenue is probably the most effective.
An empty building deteriorates; an occupied building is maintained by those who use it.
Thus, preserving does not mean freezing.
Many of the buildings we admire have changed function several times over the centuries.
What we call heritage is often the result of a long series of repurposings.

sentences: Do what you love and you will never work a single day." This phrase is widely circulated.
It deserves to be examined, as it is more recent and more problematic than it seems.
For most of history, work was not meant to be fulfilling.
It served to meet basic needs.
The idea that a job should provide meaning and personal fulfillment emerged late, especially in certain professional categories.
This evolution has its benefits: it has legitimized the refusal of degrading conditions.
But it also produces perverse effects.
The first is guilt.
If work is supposed to be a passion, not loving your own becomes a personal failure rather than an ordinary situation.
However, the majority of jobs, in any society, are necessary without being exciting.
The second effect is more concrete.
The sectors where passion is emphasized — culture, care, entertainment, research, sports — are often those where pay is the lowest and conditions are the hardest.
The supposed passion serves as an implicit argument: since you love this, you will accept less.
Researchers have named this phenomenon and documented it in several countries.
Should we then give up on seeking meaning?
Certainly not.
But perhaps we should shift the demand.
A job can be bearable and well-paid, leaving time and energy for what matters elsewhere.
This is not a renunciation.
It's another way to refuse that work takes up all the space.

sentences: There is a system that simultaneously addresses two distinct problems: student housing, which is expensive and scarce in large cities, and the isolation of elderly people living alone in homes that have become too large.
The principle of intergenerational cohabitation is simple.

A student is housed with an elderly person for a very low rent, sometimes free, in exchange for regular companionship and small services: sharing a few meals, being there in the evening, helping with shopping or a device.
This is not a home care job.
The student does not provide any medical care or heavy tasks, and this is an essential distinction, regularly emphasized by the associations that organize these pairings.
These associations also play a crucial role.
They check the accommodations, meet both parties, establish a written agreement specifying the commitments, and intervene in case of difficulties.
Experiences conducted without a framework fail much more often: implicit expectations diverge, no one dares to talk about it, and the situation deteriorates.
Feedback from participants is mostly positive, with a common point: the benefits are not what was expected.
Students mention less the savings on rent than the conversations.
Elderly people mention less the security than having someone to share their day with.
The system remains modest in number, limited by logistics and by the understandable reluctance to let a stranger into one's home.
But it illustrates a useful idea.
Some social problems cannot be solved separately.
They are resolved by bringing them together.

sentences: Hiccups are a common phenomenon, somewhat ridiculous, and scientifically more mysterious than we might think.
They result from a sudden and involuntary contraction of the diaphragm, this large muscle located under the lungs that controls breathing.
This contraction causes a sudden inhalation, immediately stopped by the quick closure of the throat — hence the characteristic little sound.
Most episodes are benign and triggered by identifiable causes: eating too quickly, drinking carbonated beverages, a sudden change in temperature, or sometimes an emotion.
The real question lies elsewhere: what is the purpose of hiccups?
And the honest answer is that we don't know.
Unlike coughing or sneezing, which protect the body, hiccups seem to have no useful function.
Some researchers see it as a remnant of our distant evolutionary history, with no current use.
There are countless home remedies: holding your breath, drinking water upside down, being surprised.
Interestingly, many of them actually work, but for a common reason.
Hiccups are maintained by a reflex.
Several of these methods act on the same mechanism: they increase the level of carbon dioxide in the blood, or they stimulate nerves that interrupt the cycle.
Holding your breath does both at once.
This explains why there is no single remedy: several paths lead to the same result.
In very rare cases, hiccups can persist for days or even weeks, indicating a medical problem.
But for the vast majority of us, it remains what it is: a strange reminder that our body sometimes does things for no reason.

sentences: Public art has a unique characteristic: no one has chosen it individually, and everyone sees it.
A statue in a square, a mural on a wall, a sculpture in front of a train station are all imposed on everyone, whether we like them or not.
This explains why these works provoke such lively debates.
For a work displayed in a museum, we can choose not to go see it.
A work in the street, we encounter it every day.
It belongs to the common space, and everyone feels entitled to give their opinion — which is healthy.
The controversies revolve around several aspects.
The first is aesthetic: a contemporary work placed in an old neighborhood almost always divides opinion.
Some see it as a welcome boldness, others as a visual aggression.
The second is financial: spending public money on art raises the question, 'Wasn't there something more urgent?'
A legitimate question, but one that assumes the beauty of a common place would never be a priority.
The third is memorial, and it is the most intense today.
The statues erected in the past honor figures whose perception has changed.
Should they be removed, explained, or left as they are?
The debate pits those who want to erase against those who want to contextualize.
These conflicts, as exhausting as they may be, have a virtue.
They force a community to ask itself what it values, what it wants to remember, and what it wants to show about itself.
A city without public art would be quieter.
It would also convey something sadder: that the common space deserves only the useful.

sentences: We set off, or so we think, to discover the elsewhere: different landscapes, different customs, different ways of living.
And it's true that travel allows us to discover all of this.
But its deepest effect may lie elsewhere: by confronting us with other ways of being, it reveals to us, in return, our own way of being, which we had until then taken for the only natural one.
The stranger is a mirror, and it's often ourselves that we end up seeing in it.
The mechanism is subtle.
As long as we only know our own world, we do not perceive it as one possibility among others, but as the very evidence.
Our habits, our values, our ways of eating, greeting, conceiving time or family seem self-evident to us, because we have never seen that they could be different.
It is by discovering that elsewhere people do, think, and live differently that we simultaneously discover that our own ways are not inevitable.
This revelation can be destabilizing, and that is its virtue.
Seeing that others organize their existence on different principles, and do not live any worse for it, shakes our certainties.
What we took for natural turns out to be cultural; what we believed to be universal is revealed to be particular.
Travel, in this sense, is a lesson in humility: it teaches us that our way of seeing the world is just one way among others, neither the only one nor necessarily the best.
But this confrontation can also be a lesson in recognition.
By discovering other ways of living, we do not necessarily give up our own; sometimes, we rediscover them, understand them better, and appreciate their value that habit had hidden from us.
We return from afar, seeing our own home with fresh eyes, finally able to appreciate or question what we no longer even noticed.
That is why true travel requires a particular disposition: that of being open to questioning.
The traveler who judges everything by the standard of their own habits, who finds what differs from them 'strange' or 'backward', will see in the stranger only a deviation from their norm.
They are not really traveling: they are carrying their world with them.
Traveling, on the contrary, is to accept, for a time, to see with other eyes.
The greatest benefit of travel may therefore not be what it allows us to discover about the world, but what it helps us discover about ourselves.
We set off in search of the elsewhere; we return with a bit more clarity about ourselves.
The stranger, indeed, is the best of mirrors.

sentences: “To remember so that it does not happen again.” This phrase, often repeated regarding the great tragedies of history, expresses a deep conviction: the memory of past horrors would protect us against their return.
It is in the name of this idea that we maintain the memory of massacres, that we visit places of horror, that we pass on to younger generations the story of the worst.
But this conviction, noble as it may be, deserves to be examined with clarity.
Does memory really suffice to prevent the worst from happening again?
The idea is based on a seductive reasoning: if people know what certain ideas, certain hatreds, and certain cowardices have led to, they will be able to recognize and reject them.
Memory would thus be a vigilance, an immunity acquired at the cost of past misfortunes.
And it is true that ignorance of the past encourages its repetition: a people who knows nothing of the disasters of history would be more exposed to repeating the same path.
In this respect, memory is indeed a protection, and forgetting is a danger.
However, history itself invites us not to overestimate this power.
For atrocities have been repeated even when the memory of previous ones was vivid.
Knowing the past has not always prevented repetition, and we have seen educated societies succumb to horror once again.
Memory alone does not provide immunity.
It can even, if misdirected, foster new resentments, sustain old hatreds, and serve to justify new violence in the name of past wounds.
Memory is not always on the side of peace.
This is because memory can take very different forms.
Remembering as a victim, to nurture a grudge, does not have the same effect as remembering to understand.
A memory that merely rehashes emotion, without an effort to understand, offers poor protection: it stirs without enlightening.
What truly protects is less the raw memory than what we make of it: understanding how the worst was possible, what mechanisms led to it, and what ordinary cowardices allowed it.
Simply remembering the facts is not enough; we must draw intelligence from them.
Memory is therefore a protection only under certain conditions.
It must be accompanied by understanding, aimed at recognizing the mechanisms of evil rather than just mourning the victims, and it should illuminate the present rather than confine us to the past.
An intelligent memory looks less backward than forward: it scrutinizes the present to detect the signs of what it knows.
To remember so as not to repeat: yes, but only if we truly remember, that is, if we understand.
Memory is not an automatic guarantee; it is a vigilance to be maintained, a task always to be resumed.
It only protects us if we make it work, not if we let it lie dormant in commemorations.

sentences: Almost everyone claims to believe in justice.
No one openly defends injustice, and "that's not fair" is among the most universal protests.
However, as soon as we try to define what a just society is, agreement falls apart.
For under the same word lie profoundly different conceptions, and disagreement about justice may be the most fundamental issue in political life.
Understanding this disagreement is key to grasping the essence of our divisions.
Let's take a seemingly simple question: how should the wealth produced by a society be distributed fairly?
One initial answer is: to each according to their merit.
It would be fair for those who work harder, take more risks, and contribute more to receive more.
Rewarding effort and talent, allowing everyone to keep the fruits of their labor: this is, for many, the very demand of justice.
According to this view, inequalities are not unjust in themselves, as long as they reflect different merits.
A second answer challenges this perspective.
Merit, it says, is not as pure as it seems: those who succeed owe much to factors beyond their control — their birth, their background, their innate talents, and luck.
Is it fair that someone who had the luck to be born into a favorable environment reaps the rewards throughout their life, while another, born into poverty, bears all the burden?
According to this conception, a just society must correct inequalities that do not result from individuals' choices but from the lottery of birth.
Justice then requires a form of redistribution.
A third answer shifts the question further.
What matters, it says, is not so much the distribution of wealth as the guarantee, for everyone, of a minimum of dignity and freedom.
A just society would be one where no one lacks the essentials, where everyone can live decently and lead the life they have reason to want, regardless of other inequalities.
The emphasis is less on equality than on a threshold below which it would be undignified to let anyone fall.
These conceptions are not mere arbitrary opinions; each is based on respectable values — freedom, equality, dignity, responsibility — all of which matter, but which come into tension.
One cannot maximize both the reward for merit and the correction of birth inequalities; it requires arbitration, and it is in this arbitration that our disagreements lie.
Those who oppose each other on justice are not, most often, one side just and the other not: they assign different weights to equally legitimate values.
Recognizing this does not resolve the disagreement, but makes it more fruitful.
It allows us to stop seeing the opponent as an enemy of justice, and to understand that they have a different conception based on other priorities.

A just society may not be one that has found the definitive formula for justice — there isn't one — but one that knows how to debate these tensions without resolving them through force, and seeks, without ever fully achieving it, a balance among all these real demands.

sentences: One of the deepest differences between France and Great Britain lies in the role they assign to the State.
In France, a lot is expected from the public authority: to protect, to organize, to guarantee education, health, and security for everyone.
In Great Britain, despite a public health system that the British are very attached to, there is more trust in individual initiative, the market, and personal responsibility.
These two attitudes, both respectable, reflect two conceptions of society.
The French tradition is marked by a long history of centralization.
For centuries, the State has played a driving role, shaping the nation, unifying the territory, and organizing collective life.
From this history has arisen a reflex: when faced with a problem, people turn to the State, expect it to act, and blame it for not doing enough.
The State is seen as the guarantor of the general interest, above individual interests, and there is a strong desire for it to provide protection that the market alone would not guarantee.
The British tradition is different.
It is more suspicious of the concentration of power, values individual autonomy, and trusts civil society and private initiative to solve many problems.
The State is perceived less as a natural protector than as a force that needs to be limited, for fear it might encroach on freedoms.
People expect individuals to take charge of themselves, not to rely primarily on the community, and see entrepreneurial spirit as a cardinal virtue.
Both visions have their strengths and weaknesses.

The French model offers extensive protection, reduces certain inequalities, and ensures a security that many envy; however, it is sometimes criticized for being burdensome, stifling initiative, and fostering excessive expectations of the State among citizens.
The British model allows more room for initiative, flexibility, and dynamism; but it is criticized for allowing inequalities to widen and for abandoning the weakest to an indifferent market.
Each model pays for its virtues with corresponding flaws.

It would be futile to decree which is superior, as they address questions on which legitimate values diverge: how much security, how much freedom; how much imposed solidarity, how much individual responsibility.
These are trade-offs, not truths, and each society decides based on its history and preferences.
The French person attached to the State and the British person attached to initiative are not wrong or right; they prioritize different goods.
Observing these two models helps us understand that there is not just one right way to organize a society, but choices that reflect values.

And it is also, for each, an opportunity to better see their own model: the French, by discovering the British attachment to autonomy, realizes what is unique about their preference for the State; the British, by discovering French protection, may question what their individualism overlooks.
Each neighbor is, for the other, a revealing mirror.

sentences: Night is frightening, and this fear, as old as humanity itself, shapes our relationship with the nocturnal city.
Many people don't dare to go out at night, or only in certain places, avoiding dark streets and hurrying their pace.
This fear is not without foundation, but it deserves to be questioned: what exactly are we afraid of in the night?
And does this fear reflect a real danger, or does it tell us more about ourselves than about the night?
The fear of the night has very deep roots.
For most of its history, humanity was vulnerable at night: deprived of sight, exposed to predators and the dangers of darkness.
This ancestral fear, ingrained in us, persists even though its original causes have largely disappeared.
We no longer really fear wild animals in our streets, but darkness continues to worry us, awakening an anxiety older than reason.
In the city, however, the fear of the night has shifted: it is no longer the darkness itself that we dread, but what it might hide — and especially, other people.

Urban nights are frightening because they are populated by strangers whose intentions we do not know, because they are believed to harbor threats, aggression, and danger from others who have become invisible and unpredictable.
The fear of the dark has largely become the fear of others, of those we imagine lurking in the shadows.
This fear is partly justified: the night has its share of real dangers, and it would be naive to deny that.
But it is also, to a large extent, a construct, fed by imagination, stories, and a perception of risk that is often exaggerated.
Studies show that the feeling of nighttime insecurity far exceeds real dangers, and it mainly affects those who are, in reality, the least exposed.
We are afraid well beyond what reality justifies, and this excessive fear has effects of its own.
For the fear of the night transforms the city.
By avoiding dark streets, we make them even more frightening, because an empty street is scarier than a lively one.
Fear thus feeds on itself: the less we go out, the more threatening the night seems, and the more we stay at home.
It also affects people unevenly: some, due to their circumstances, feel more vulnerable and see the night closing in on them, while others move freely through it.
Nighttime fear draws invisible boundaries, excludes, and restricts the freedom to move.
Questioning the fear of the night does not mean denying its dangers, but refusing to let it govern us beyond what reality justifies.

It also means understanding that nighttime safety is not achieved only by lighting up the streets or increasing surveillance, but by bringing life back to them: for a lively, inhabited, shared nocturnal city is safer than one deserted by fear.
Reclaiming the night is perhaps, first and foremost, about stopping being afraid of each other.

sentences: Medicine continues to push back the boundaries of death.
What was fatal yesterday can be treated today; life expectancy has spectacularly increased, and some even dream of extending it indefinitely, or even abolishing death one day.
In light of these prospects, a question, long theoretical, arises with new urgency: should we want to live longer and longer?
Does the desire to push back death, as natural as it may be, have a limit that it would be wise to recognize?
The desire to live is the most fundamental there is, and it would be absurd to condemn it.
That medicine has so greatly delayed early death, spared so much suffering and mourning, is an undeniable blessing.
No one seriously wishes to return to a time when people died young, when illness struck without recourse.
Wanting to live, and to live healthily for as long as possible, is legitimate, and the advances that make this possible deserve to be praised.
The question is therefore not about renouncing this desire, but about knowing whether it has a point beyond which it would turn back.
For extending life only makes sense if this prolonged life remains worthy of being lived.
Pushing back death at the cost of a diminished, dependent existence, devoid of what makes life valuable, is not necessarily progress.
Extending duration without extending quality can be a cruelty rather than a blessing.
That is why the real question may not be 'how long?', but 'what kind of life?' — not the number of years, but what they contain.
Adding years to life is only worthwhile if one also adds life to those years.
There is something even more dizzying: the idea of a life without end.
Some dream of abolishing death itself.
But would that really be desirable?
One can doubt it.
Many thinkers have argued that death, far from being merely an evil, gives life a part of its meaning and flavor.
It is because our time is limited that each moment has value, that we choose, that we commit.
An infinite existence, where nothing would ever be urgent, where everything could always be postponed, might lose what makes life precious: its irreplaceable and finite nature.
Death is not only what deprives us of life; it is also, paradoxically, what gives it weight.
This does not mean we should stop pushing back death, nor renounce the advances that extend and improve life.
It means not to make duration an absolute, as if living longer and longer were in itself the ultimate goal.
An ancient wisdom taught that we should seek less to add days to our lives than to give life to our days.
This distinction remains valuable at a time when medicine gives us unprecedented powers over the duration of existence.
Should we want to live longer and longer?
Yes, as long as it is about living fully, healthily, in a life that is worthwhile.
But perhaps not to the point of making duration everything, nor dreaming of an immortality that, by abolishing death, would also abolish what gives life its value.
Living well matters more than living long — and wisdom may consist in accepting that our time is limited, while still cherishing every moment it grants us.

sentences: We live in the certainty of being free.
We deliberate, we choose, we hold others and ourselves accountable for our actions; our entire moral and social life rests on this conviction.
And yet, an old doubt undermines it, which modern science has revived.

If every event has a cause, if the world obeys a chain of causes and effects, then our choices, which are also events, have their own causes; they result from the state of our brain, our history, and our dispositions, which themselves stem from prior causes.
Where, in this chain, can true freedom reside?
Could the feeling we have of it be nothing but an illusion?
The argument is formidable in its simplicity.
When I believe I am choosing freely, I am merely executing what the prior state of the world and myself made inevitable.
My deliberation itself, my reasons, my feeling of deciding, are the effects of causes that I do not control.

The freedom I attribute to myself would be nothing but ignorance of the causes that determine me: I believe I am free because I do not see what makes me act, like a stone that would think it is free if it were unaware of gravity.
This thesis, determinism, has for it the coherence and support of everything science teaches us about the chain of causes.
Should we then renounce freedom?
Before conceding this, it is important to examine what we mean by this word.

If being free means escaping all cause, acting without anything determining our action, then freedom is indeed impossible, and perhaps even unintelligible: an action without any cause would not be a free act, but pure chance, which is not what we seek either.
Freedom as total absence of determination is a chimera; but is that really what we mean when we say we are free?
Another conception is possible, which does not place freedom outside of causes, but within a certain way of being caused.

I am free, according to this view, not when nothing determines me, but when what determines me is myself: my own reasons, my values, my reflection, as opposed to external constraint or an impulse I suffer.

A person forced against their will is not free; someone acting under the influence of a passion that overwhelms them is hardly free; but someone who acts according to what they judge, after deliberation, to be best, is free in a real sense, even if their deliberation itself has causes.
Freedom would not be the absence of causes, but the alignment of the act with the self that performs it.
This conception does not dispel all difficulty, as one might object that this self, with its reasons and values, is the product of causes it did not choose.
The debate here cannot be settled with a single word, and it would be presumptuous to claim to close it.
But it is important to note this: even someone who theoretically persuades themselves that freedom is illusory continues, in practice, to deliberate, to choose, to hold others accountable.
They cannot live according to their thesis.

This impossibility is not proof, but it indicates that freedom, whatever one thinks of its metaphysical status, is a category we cannot rid ourselves of, inscribed at the heart of our experience and our shared life.
Perhaps the question is not whether we are free in the absolute sense — a question that might have no answer — but rather to recognize the degrees of freedom that make a real difference in our lives.

Between the person dominated by their impulses and the one who masters them, between the one who follows blindly and the one who reflects, between the slave and the free person, there are differences that no determinism erases.

Cultivating these differences, increasing within oneself the part of what acts by reason rather than by constraint, is perhaps what it means to be free: not to escape causes, but to become increasingly the cause of one's own actions.

sentences: The expression 'duty of memory' has become established to designate the obligation to remember the great tragedies of the past, particularly mass crimes, in order to honor them and prevent their recurrence.

This obligation is just and necessary: to forget the victims, to erase the crimes, would be a second injustice, and a society that knows nothing of its own abysses would be more exposed to falling back into them.
And yet, the duty of memory, elevated to an indisputable imperative, has limits and paradoxes that require the courage to examine, not to reject it, but to clarify its meaning.
The first difficulty lies in the relationship between memory and history.

Memory is not history: it is laden with emotion, directed towards the victims, guided by the duty of fidelity; history aims for understanding, context, and explanation, with the distance that this entails.
However, if the duty of memory dominates without sharing, it can come into tension with the work of the historian.
Understanding how a crime was possible, analyzing its mechanisms coldly, may seem disrespectful to the victims, even slipping into excuse.
But to renounce understanding in the name of memory is to deprive oneself precisely of what could prevent the return of the worst: for we can only prevent what we have understood.
The second difficulty lies in the selection of memory.
We cannot commemorate everything with the same intensity; memory, like history, chooses.
However, this choice is not neutral: some victims are abundantly remembered, others forgotten; some crimes occupy public space, while others remain in the shadows.

This inequality of memory can lead to painful competitions, with each group demanding equivalent recognition for its own suffering, risking an escalation where the memory of some seems to be at the expense of others.
The duty of memory, intended to unite in reflection, can thus become a ground for conflict.
The third difficulty, deeper, concerns the very effectiveness of memory.
It is assumed that remembering protects against repetition.
But history partly disproves this reassuring assumption: atrocities have recurred despite the vivid memory of previous ones, and commemoration has not always prevented new crimes.
Memory alone does not vaccinate.
Worse, a poorly directed memory can foster new resentments, sustain hatreds, and serve to justify present violence in the name of past suffering.
Remembering is not always on the side of peace; it all depends on what we do with that memory.
Should we then relativize the duty of memory?
No, but we should think of it differently.

It is not about remembering less, but about remembering better: linking memory to understanding, rather than opposing them; aiming, through the memory of the victims, for an understanding of the mechanisms that made the crime possible; making memory not a fixed cult, turned towards the past, but an active vigilance, directed towards the present.

A memory that serves only to commemorate, without enlightening or preventing, would fail its purpose; a memory that makes us attentive to the warning signs, in the present, of what it recalls from the past, would truly fulfill its role.
The duty of memory, when well understood, is therefore not the duty to reiterate, but the duty to understand in order to remain vigilant.
It does not oppose history; it calls for it.

Honoring the victims, yes, but also understanding the perpetrators, not to excuse them, but to recognize, in ordinary humanity, the possibility of the worst — for it is this recognition, more than commemorative emotion, that can arm us.
Memory without understanding is a sterile piety; understanding without memory is a culpable coldness.
It is from their union that what the duty of memory truly aims for can arise: not only to not forget, but to not repeat.

sentences: Our time is egalitarian, and in many ways, that's a progress.
It rejects imposed hierarchies, considers everyone equal to one another, and values everyone's right to express their opinion.
However, this egalitarian spirit, admirable in terms of rights and dignity, sometimes extends to areas where it doesn't belong: the realm of facts and knowledge.
Thus, we slide from the correct idea that all citizens are equal in dignity to the false idea that all opinions are equally valid, even on factual matters where expertise exists.
This shift, which flatters our democratic sensibility, deserves to be questioned, as it has serious consequences.
First, we must affirm an obvious truth that our time tends to obscure: on factual matters, not all opinions are equal.
The opinion of someone who has studied a subject for years, who masters the data, methods, and debates, is not worth the same as that of someone who has never thought about it.
This does not make one person superior to the other; it simply means that, on this specific subject, one knows and the other does not.
Denying this difference in the name of equality confuses the equality of persons with a supposed equality of knowledge, which does not exist.
That everyone has the right to express their opinion does not mean that all opinions are equally well-founded.
This confusion is exacerbated by a phenomenon unique to our time: universal access to information gives everyone the illusion of competence.
Having consulted a few sources and read a few articles, anyone can believe they are capable of judging issues that actually require years of study.

This illusion is all the more persistent because those who know little do not grasp the extent of what they ignore: one must already have some knowledge to perceive the complexity of a field, and the ignorant, precisely because they are ignorant, overestimate their own competence.
Thus, a distrust of experts spreads, in the name of a "I form my own opinion" that confuses the autonomy of judgment with the presumption of ignorance.
Should we then conclude that we must blindly rely on experts, and that ordinary citizens should just remain silent?
That would be falling into the opposite excess, which is equally dangerous.
For recognizing the authority of knowledge does not mean abdicating all judgment.
Experts can be wrong, be influenced by interests, or step outside their area of expertise; their words deserve respect, not submission.

Moreover, while science establishes facts, it does not decide what to do with them: choices that involve values — what to do with what science establishes — fall within the realm of democratic debate, where everyone's opinion legitimately counts.
Expertise has authority over facts, not over ends.
It is this distinction that allows us to escape the false dilemma between contempt for experts and blind submission.
On factual matters, competence has legitimate authority, and denying it in the name of equality is unreasonable.
On issues of values and collective choices, however, no expert should decide in place of citizens, and the equality of voices reasserts its rights.

Confusing these two realms — wanting experts to decide on ends, or citizens to determine facts solely by their opinion — leads to two dead ends: technocracy that disempowers citizens, or populism that scorns knowledge.
Defending the idea that, on facts, not all opinions are equal does not betray the democratic spirit; it preserves it from its own drift.

A democracy does not need citizens who all believe they are experts, but rather citizens capable of recognizing what they know and what they do not know, of trusting knowledge where it is well-founded, while maintaining their full authority over choices that pertain to values.

The equality of persons does not require the equality of knowledge; it instead demands that we distinguish, so that democratic debate is based on the best-established facts, and not on the confusion of all opinions.
Respecting knowledge does not mean renouncing one's freedom as a citizen; it means using it wisely.

sentences: On Saturday morning, I had a long list of things to do in town.
Six things exactly.

I had everything written down on a piece of paper: - go to the post office - stop by the bank - buy some bread - pick up my shoes at the cobbler - get a medicine at the pharmacy - buy a gift for Chloé.
Before leaving, I thought about the order.
It's important; otherwise, you walk down the same street twice.
The post office and the bank are in the same square.
I started there.
I left at nine o'clock.
It was cool, but the sun was shining.
First, the post office.
There was a line of seven people!
I waited twenty minutes.
Then, the bank, right across: it was quicker.
After that, I went to the cobbler.
My shoes were ready, and he only charged me twelve euros.
Then the pharmacy, where the pharmacist explained the medicine to me well.
Next, the toy store for my niece's gift.
I hesitated for a long time, then I chose a construction game.
Finally, the bakery.
But when I arrived, there was a sign on the door: 'Closed on Saturday afternoons.'
It was a quarter past one.
Too late!
Five things out of six.
For the bread, it will be tomorrow.

sentences: In France, sales happen twice a year: in January and June.
The dates are set by law, and they are the same for all stores.
On the first day of sales, there are a lot of people in the city.
Some people wait in front of the stores before they open.
Last Saturday, I went there with my friend Léa.
We needed winter coats.
In the first store, it was impossible: there were too many people.
The clothes were everywhere, even on the floor.
The fitting rooms had a wait of twenty minutes.
Léa found a coat at fifty percent off.
It was blue, warm, and it looked great on her.
Original price: one hundred forty euros.
Sale price: seventy euros.
As for me, I didn't find anything in my size.
Medium sizes always sell out first.
So I made a mistake.
I bought a shirt that I didn't like very much, simply because it cost twelve euros instead of forty.
On the bus, Léa asked me: 'Are you going to wear it?'
I thought about it.
'Maybe not.'
'Then it's not a saving.
It's an expense.'
She was right.
A cheap thing that you don't wear ends up costing a lot.
The shirt is still in my closet, with the tag.

sentences: Nothing is more familiar to us than time, and nothing is more difficult to think about.
What is time, then?

If no one asks me, I know it; if I want to explain it to someone who asks me, I no longer know it." This admission from an ancient thinker expresses the strange paradox of our relationship with time: we are immersed in it, we live it every moment, and yet, as soon as we try to grasp it, it slips away.
Let's probe this enigma starting from a dizzying observation: upon closer inspection, time seems to have no reality, each of its three dimensions dissolving under analysis.
Let's consider the past.
It was, but it is no longer; it has ceased to exist, it has only the fragile being of memory.
What is past no longer exists anywhere, except in the trace it has left in us; the past, as such, has no present being.
Let's consider the future.
It will be, but it is not yet; it has only the uncertain being of expectation.
What is to come does not exist yet, it is only anticipated, imagined, foreseen; the future, as such, also has no present being.
Only the present remains, the only one that seems to exist.
But what is the present?

A moment, one might say; but this moment, if we grasp it, reveals itself to be without thickness, a pure limit between a past that is no longer and a future that is not yet, an elusive point that vanishes as soon as we try to fix it.
The present, scarcely is it, that it is already no more; it does not last, it passes, it flees.
Thus time, whose three dimensions dissolve — the past that is no longer, the future that is not yet, the present that vanishes — seems to have no reality, to be a pure flight without substance.
This vertigo is not a mere play of the mind; it touches on something real in our experience of time, which is indeed that of a flight, a flow that nothing stops.
We experience time as something that escapes us, something we cannot hold onto, that carries everything away — our days, our joys, our loved ones, ourselves.
Time is what passes, and its flight is the source of many of our anxieties: we would like to hold onto what flees, to stop the happy moment, to preserve what time tears from us, and we cannot.

The apparent unreality of time, this dissolution of its dimensions, philosophically expresses what we experience existentially: that time cannot be grasped, that it slips through our fingers, that it is pure flight.
And yet, time is not nothing; it is even, in a sense, the most real thing in our experience.
For if its dimensions dissolve when we consider them as things, time fully exists as lived, as the very fabric of our existence.

A thinker has suggested that time does not exist outside, as an objective thing, but in the soul, as a relationship to what is no longer and to what is not yet: the past exists as present memory, the future as present expectation, the present as attention.
Time would not be an external reality, but a dimension of consciousness, the way a mind retains the past, awaits the future, and stands in the present.
Thus time, unreal as a thing, would be fully real as lived.
This conception shifts the vertigo without completely dispelling it, but it sheds light on our relationship with time.
If time is primarily lived, then our way of living it matters more than its objective nature.
We can inhabit time in various ways: fleeing the present by living in nostalgia for the past or anxiety for the future; or conversely, standing in the present, the only place where we truly live.
For if the past is no longer and the future not yet, it is indeed in the present, however fleeting it may be, that our life unfolds; it is the only time we truly have.

All wisdom regarding time perhaps lies here: not to abandon the present, the only real one, in favor of a bygone past or an uncertain future, but to fully inhabit the fleeting moment, since it is in it, and in it alone, that we exist.
The present, one might say, does not exist, since it vanishes as soon as we grasp it.

But perhaps the opposite should be concluded: that the present, however fleeting it may be, is the only place of reality, the only time where we truly live, and that wisdom consists not in holding onto it — which is impossible — but in inhabiting it.
Time escapes us if we want to grasp it as a thing; it reveals itself to us if we consent to live it as a flow.

And living, at its core, may be nothing other than this: consenting to the flight of time while fully inhabiting each of its moments — accepting that we cannot hold onto the present, and loving it all the more as it passes.

sentences: There is a riddle at the heart of all power, so obvious that we no longer see it, yet vertiginous as soon as we articulate it: why does the many obey the few?
How is it that a multitude submits to a handful, who could not, by sheer force, compel them all?

A thinker, centuries ago, posed this question with an acuity that has lost none of its force: whence comes it that so many men obey one alone, not by insurmountable constraint, but as if they consented, as if they desired their own servitude?
This riddle of voluntary servitude touches on the deepest mystery of power.
The observation that underpins it is striking.
A tyrant, however powerful he may be, has power only to the extent that it is granted to him by those who obey him; his strength is merely theirs, turned against them.
If they all ceased to obey, he would be nothing; his domination rests entirely on their consent, whether active or resigned.
How is it, then, that they obey, that they themselves support the one who oppresses them, that they provide the power that crushes them?

The power of the few over the many is a riddle, for the many could rid themselves of the few simply by ceasing to obey; and yet they obey, they submit, they consent, in a sense, to their own servitude.
How can we explain this paradox?
Several factors come together, all of which illuminate the deep mechanisms of domination.
First, there is habit: we obey because we have always obeyed, because submission has become second nature, because the established order seems self-evident.
The habituation to servitude means that we no longer perceive it as such, that we consider it the natural state of things.
Next, there are the legitimizing narratives we have mentioned: we obey because we believe the power to be legitimate, because the narrative that justifies it has been internalized.
There is also the division among those who obey: the many could only rid themselves of the few by uniting, yet they are divided, each obeying in isolation, unable to coordinate with one another.
But perhaps the deepest mechanism of voluntary servitude lies elsewhere, in a subtle complicity between power and those who obey it.

For power is maintained not only by the constraint from above, but by a chain of complicities that runs through society: each person oppresses those who are subject to them and submits to those who dominate them, deriving from their own servitude a power over others.
Thus, domination is not only imposed from above; it is relayed, maintained, reproduced by a multitude that finds its own benefit in it, participating in servitude by drawing a share of power from it.
Voluntary servitude is not only suffered; it is, at all levels, maintained by those who endure it, in a general complicity that strengthens power.
This analysis has both a disenchanted and liberating significance.

Disenchanted, because it reveals that domination does not rest solely on the violence of the dominators, but on the complicity of the dominated, on their habits, beliefs, divisions, and their self-interested participation in the order that oppresses them.
There are not oppressors on one side and innocent oppressed on the other; there is a chain of servitude in which everyone has their share.
Liberating, because if power rests on the consent of those who obey, then that consent can be withdrawn; if servitude is voluntary, in a sense, then freedom is within reach, in the refusal to obey.

The thinker who posed this riddle drew this vertiginous conclusion: to free oneself from a tyrant, there is no need to fight him; it is enough to stop supporting him; if we refuse him obedience, he will fall by himself.

This conclusion, while it undoubtedly simplifies the reality of power relations, points to an essential truth: that power, even the most oppressive, depends on those it oppresses, and that its strength is that which they lend to it.

Understanding voluntary servitude means understanding that domination is never a pure fatality imposed from the outside, but always, to some extent, maintained by the consent, habit, and complicity of those who endure it.
And it is to discover that freedom begins with the awareness of this servitude, with the refusal to consider it natural, with the reclaiming of the consent that one had, unknowingly, granted.
The deepest servitude is that which one no longer perceives as such; the first liberation is to recognize it.

sentences: Where does the desire to know come from?
One might think it arises from need, utility, or the necessity to master the world in order to survive.
This explanation has some truth to it, but it misses the essential point that ancient thinkers recognized, placing at the origin of knowledge not need, but wonder, the amazement at what is.

"It is through wonder that men began to philosophize," said a philosopher; and this intuition, so ancient, touches on something profound about the nature of the desire to know and what truly drives it.
What is this wonder that would be at the origin of knowledge?
It is not the anxiety over a practical problem to solve, nor the need to control what threatens.
It is a more free, more disinterested movement: the wonder at the very fact that things exist, that they are what they are, that there is a world rather than nothing.
It is the astonishment at what, ceasing to be taken for granted, suddenly appears worthy of questioning, as mysterious, as calling for an explanation.

Wonder arises when what was familiar to us, which we took for granted, suddenly reveals itself as strange, remarkable, enigmatic; when we stop passing through the world without seeing it to pause, struck, at the fact that it is.
This wonder has something paradoxical about it: it often concerns the most ordinary, the most familiar things, precisely those that habit makes us stop seeing.
A child is amazed by everything because everything is new to him; the adult, accustomed, stops being amazed, passes through the world without seeing it, takes everything for granted.
To rediscover wonder is, in a sense, to regain a fresh perspective on what habit has dulled, to see again as remarkable what had become invisible through familiarity.
Knowledge arises from this ability to be amazed by what is taken for granted, to find mysterious what one thought one knew, to question what one no longer saw.
Understanding that knowledge arises from wonder, and not just from need, has important consequences.
This means that the highest, most disinterested knowledge does not stem from utility but from gratuitousness, from the desire to understand for the sake of understanding, regardless of any profit.
The deepest science and philosophy did not arise from the need to control, but from the wonder at what is, from the free desire to understand the world and our place in it.

That is why reducing knowledge to its utility, valuing knowledge only for its applications, is to misunderstand what most deeply animates it: not need, but wonder; not interest, but disinterested astonishment at the mystery of what is.
This also means that wonder is not only at the origin of knowledge, but that it remains its driving force and perhaps its end.

For knowledge, if it arises from wonder, does not necessarily dissipate it; the greatest scholars often testify to a wonder that grows with their knowledge, as if understanding more only deepens the mystery.
Science does not kill wonder; it nourishes it, revealing a world broader, more complex, and more mysterious than one could imagine.
Wonder is not only the beginning of knowledge, abolished by it; it is its permanent companion, rekindled with each discovery, deepened by each advancement.
The true scholar is one who knows how to marvel.
Cultivating wonder, regaining the ability to be amazed by what is, is therefore more than a pleasant disposition; it is reconnecting with the very source of the desire to know and understand.

In a world where habit, routine, and information saturation tend to dull our capacity for wonder, where everything is treated as self-evident, known, available, rediscovering wonder is a form of resistance and life.
It is relearning to see the world as remarkable, to find mysterious what one thought one knew, to be astonished by the very fact that things exist.

And this capacity for wonder is not only what animates knowledge; it is also what makes the world habitable, what keeps us from the boredom of those who think they know everything, what keeps alive the joy of understanding.
To still marvel, despite everything one knows or thinks one knows, may be the sign of a mind that remains alive — and the condition for all true knowledge.

sentences: Everything happened because of my colleague Nadia.
In September, she told me, "I'm starting a dance class on Tuesday evenings.
Come with me!" I said no, she insisted, and I said no again.
Then she promised to treat me to a restaurant.
I said yes.
The first class was a disaster.
There were fifteen beginners, and I was the worst.
I turned left when everyone turned right.
I stepped on Nadia's feet twice.
I was red with shame.
It's okay!
said Madame Elena, the teacher.
Everyone starts somewhere.
The body learns slowly, but it learns.
She was right.
Week after week, something changed.
In October, I knew the basic steps.
In December, my body moved by itself, with the music, without thinking.
Nadia looked at me, surprised: "But you're dancing!"
Now, Tuesday evenings are my favorite time of the week.
In the dance studio, I forget everything: work, bills, worries.
Dance has also changed me in other ways.
I stand up straighter and I dare a little more.
At my cousin's wedding last month, I danced all evening.
Before, I would sit near the buffet.
Thank you, Nadia.
By the way, I still owe you a dinner.
I'm the one who will treat.

sentences: Desire is the driving force of our lives: we are constantly desiring, and this tension towards what we do not have moves us, pushes us, and makes us act.
But desire seems to be linked to lack: to desire is to want what we do not have, to reach for what is missing; and this connection between desire and lack appears to condemn it to dissatisfaction.
For hardly have we obtained what we desired than desire shifts, seeks a new object, and is reborn as a lack of something else.
Desire would thus be a perpetual dissatisfaction, an endless pursuit where we are always lacking.
Is this conception, deep and ancient, the truth of desire, or can it be something other than a lack destined to never be fulfilled?
The conception of desire as lack has a long history and great strength.
It faithfully describes a common experience: that desire arises from a lack, reaches towards what is missing, and shifts as soon as it is fulfilled.
According to this view, desire is essentially dissatisfaction: we only desire what we do not have, and possessing the object of desire extinguishes desire, which immediately reappears elsewhere.
Desire would therefore be a suffering, a perpetual lack, a quest doomed to failure; and wisdom would consist in freeing oneself from it, extinguishing desire to escape the dissatisfaction it brings.
This conception, taken to its conclusion, leads to a condemnation of desire and a wisdom of detachment, which seeks peace in the extinction of desire.
However, this conception, no matter how profound it may be, may not fully capture the truth of desire.
For there are desires that do not seem to be mere lacks, desires that are more about abundance than deficiency, expressions of a fullness rather than deprivation.

The desire to create, to give, to love, is not always the lack of what one does not have; it can be the overflow of what one has, the expansion of a force, the generosity of a being that overflows from within.

The artist who desires to create, the generous person who desires to give, the lover who desires the well-being of their beloved, do not necessarily lack; they express a fullness, an inner richness that spreads.
Thus, there would be two kinds of desires: the lack-desire, which aims at what is missing, and the fullness-desire, which expresses an abundance, an overflow of life.
This distinction transforms the relationship to desire.
If every desire were a lack, wisdom would be to free oneself from it; but if there exists a fullness-desire, then desire is not only to be extinguished, it can be cultivated, directed, and fulfilled.
The desire to create, to give, to love, is not a suffering to be eliminated, but a wealth to be unfolded; it does not call for detachment, but for commitment, expression, and realization.

The question is no longer to extinguish desire, but to distinguish desires, to discern those that are an insatiable lack from those that are a creative fullness, and to direct one's life towards the latter rather than allowing oneself to be consumed by the former.
This conception also sheds light on the nature of love.
For love can be either of the two desires.

There is a love that is lack, that seeks to fill a void in the other, that loves out of need, that possesses more than it gives; this love is greedy, anxious, never satisfied, because it expects the other to fill a lack that nothing can fill.

And there is a love that is fullness, that loves out of abundance, that desires the well-being of the beloved more than possession, that gives more than it takes; this love is not lack but generosity, not greed but giving.
The difference between these two loves — the lack-love that takes and the fullness-love that gives — is perhaps the deepest there is in terms of love, and it determines its value.
Thus, desire is not necessarily condemned to lack and dissatisfaction.

If it is true that a large part of our desires are lacks destined to never be fulfilled, and that regarding them a certain wisdom of detachment holds truth, there are also desires that are fullness, overflow, generosity, and that call for not extinction but fulfillment.

The wisdom regarding desire is therefore not simply to extinguish it, but to discern and direct it: to free oneself from lack-desires that devour us without fulfilling us, and to cultivate fullness-desires that express and unfold what we have of the best.

Not to desire nothing anymore, which would mean ceasing to live, but to desire differently: less out of lack than out of fullness, less to take than to give, less to fill a void than to spread a richness.
For the highest desire may not be the one that lacks and wants to possess, but the one that overflows and wants to give.

--That’s where you’re mistaken, professor,” replied Ned.

sentences: However, work is actively continuing regarding the establishment of the platforms.
The number of machines amounts to about fifty.

If Ker Karraje and engineer Serkö found themselves obliged to defend Back-Cup, three or four would be enough to secure the islet from any approach, given that they would cover an area where no ship could enter without being annihilated.

And, I wonder, isn't it likely that they will put Back-Cup in a state of defense, after reasoning as follows: In my opinion, this reasoning must have been taken even further, and these criminals must have said to themselves: "Is there a connection between this revelation, however it occurred, and the double kidnapping of Healthful-House?...
Do we know that Thomas Roch and his guard are locked up in Back-Cup?...
Do we know that this kidnapping was carried out for the benefit of the pirate Ker Karraje?...

Do Americans, English, French, Germans, and Russians have reason to fear that any forceful attack against the islet is doomed to failure?..." Yet, assuming all this is known, no matter how great the dangers may be, Ker Karraje must have understood that there would be no backing down.
A matter of utmost importance, a duty of public safety and humanity, demands the destruction of his lair.
After having once plundered the seas of the West Pacific, the pirate and his accomplices now infest the waters of the West Atlantic...
They must be destroyed at any cost!
In any case, and just considering this last hypothesis, constant surveillance is necessary for those who inhabit the cave of Back-Cup.
Thus, starting today, it is organized under the strictest conditions.
Thanks to the corridor, and without needing to go through the tunnel, the pirates keep watch outside.
Hidden among the low rocks of the coastline, they observe day and night the various points on the horizon, rising morning and evening in squads of twelve men.
Any appearance of a ship offshore, any approach of any vessel would be immediately reported.

It is evident that now, no matter how powerful their means of defense may be, even more so than a torpedo barrier, Ker Karraje, engineer Serkö, and captain Spade are troubled by issues they are trying in vain to conceal.
Thus, they have frequent meetings.
Perhaps they are discussing the question of abandoning Back-Cup while taking their riches with them, for if this retreat is known, it will surely be reduced, even if only by famine.
